subject: Machine Learning
stem: In the three-component view of a supervised learning algorithm, which component is the set of candidate functions {f_θ : θ ∈ Θ}?
options: The objective (loss) function
The optimizer
The model class (hypothesis space)
The training dataset
explanation: The model class is the set of functions the learner may choose from, indexed by the parameters θ. The objective scores how well a given f_θ fits the data, and the optimizer searches the model class for the θ that minimises that score; the objective is not itself a set of functions.
concept: Supervised learning = model class + objective + optimizer.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: The model ŷ = θ₀ + θ₁x + θ₂x² is best described as:
options: Non-linear regression, because the fitted curve is a parabola
Linear regression, because it is linear in the parameters θ
Logistic regression, because it uses a basis expansion of x
Not solvable by least squares, because x² makes the normal equations non-linear
explanation: With φ(x) = [1, x, x²], the model is ŷ = θᵀφ(x), which is linear in θ, so ordinary least squares and the normal equations apply unchanged. The parabola shape is tempting, but 'linear regression' refers to linearity in the parameters, not in the raw input.
concept: Linearity of a regression model is judged in θ, not in x.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: For logistic regression with a 0.5 threshold, the decision boundary in input space is:
options: An S-shaped curve, because the sigmoid is non-linear
The set of points where θᵀx = 0.5
The set of points where the predicted probability equals 1
The hyperplane θᵀx = 0, which is linear in x
explanation: p ≥ 0.5 exactly when σ(θᵀx) ≥ 0.5, which happens exactly when θᵀx ≥ 0, so the boundary is the linear set θᵀx = 0. The sigmoid only reshapes how the probability changes on either side; it does not bend the boundary, so the S-curve option confuses the probability surface with the boundary.
concept: Sigmoid non-linearity does not make the logistic decision boundary non-linear.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Which is the gradient descent update rule for minimising J(θ) with learning rate α?
options: θ ← θ + α∇J(θ)
θ ← θ − ∇J(θ)/α
θ ← θ − α∇J(θ)
θ ← αθ − ∇J(θ)
explanation: The gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent, so descent subtracts a step of size α along it. Adding α∇J (the sign slip) moves uphill and increases the loss.
concept: Gradient descent steps along the negative gradient, scaled by α.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: K-nearest neighbours is often called a 'lazy' learner because:
options: It stores the training data and defers almost all computation until a query arrives
It is trained with a very small learning rate
It uses only a random subset of the features
Its training phase converges slowly
explanation: KNN has essentially no training phase: it memorises the training set and computes distances to it at prediction time. It has no learning rate or iterative training, so options about slow convergence describe gradient-based learners instead.
concept: KNN is instance-based: cheap to train, expensive to predict.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: The 'naive' assumption in a Naive Bayes classifier is that:
options: Features are independent of the class label
All classes have equal prior probability
Every feature follows a Gaussian distribution
Features are conditionally independent of one another given the class
explanation: Naive Bayes factorises P(x | y) as the product of P(x_j | y), which is valid when features are independent given the class. Independence from the class label would make the features useless for classification, and Gaussian likelihoods are only one variant (Gaussian NB).
concept: Naive Bayes: P(x | y) = Π_j P(x_j | y).

subject: Machine Learning
stem: In a hard-margin SVM, the support vectors are:
options: All correctly classified training points
The training points farthest from the decision boundary
The training points lying exactly on the margin hyperplanes, where y(wᵀx + b) = 1
The misclassified training points
explanation: Support vectors have non-zero dual coefficients, and in the hard-margin case these are the points on the margin. A hard-margin SVM permits no misclassified points, and points farther away have α = 0 and do not affect the solution.
concept: Only support vectors (α > 0) determine w and b.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A trained SVM produces the score f(x) = wᵀx + b for a new point. This score is:
options: The posterior probability P(y = +1 | x)
Always a number between 0 and 1
A decision value whose sign gives the class; it is not a calibrated probability
The log-odds of class +1 by construction
explanation: An SVM is a decision machine: it predicts sign(f(x)), and f(x) can be any real number. Probabilities need a separate calibration step, such as Platt scaling, so reading f(x) as a log-odds or a posterior is wrong unless that extra step is fitted.
concept: SVM outputs are decision values, not probabilities.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: In Lloyd's K-means algorithm, the update step sets each centroid to:
options: The mean of the points currently assigned to that cluster
The medoid (an actual data point) of that cluster
The point in the cluster farthest from other centroids
The median of the whole dataset
explanation: With the assignments fixed, the centroid that minimises the within-cluster sum of squared distances is the cluster mean (set ∂J/∂μ_k = 0). Using a medoid is K-medoids, a different algorithm that restricts centres to data points.
concept: K-means update: μ_k = mean of the points in cluster k.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Which statement correctly contrasts K-means with KNN?
options: K-means is unsupervised and K is the number of clusters; KNN is supervised and K is the number of neighbours
K-means is supervised and K is the number of neighbours; KNN is unsupervised and K is the number of clusters
Both are supervised, and K is the number of classes in each
Both are unsupervised, and K is the number of features in each
explanation: K-means groups unlabelled data into K clusters, while KNN predicts a label from the K nearest labelled examples. The shared letter K is the trap: it means different things, and only KNN uses labels.
concept: K-means (clustering) and KNN (classification) share a letter, not a purpose.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A model with high bias (underfitting) typically shows:
options: Low training error and much higher validation error
High training error and a similarly high validation error
Low training error and low validation error
Validation error far below training error
explanation: An underfitting model is too simple to capture the signal, so it does badly even on the training data, and validation error is about as bad. Low training error with a large gap to validation error is the signature of high variance (overfitting), not high bias.
concept: High bias = poor fit on training and validation data alike.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Recall (sensitivity, true positive rate) is defined as:
options: TP / (TP + FP)
TP / (TP + FN)
TN / (TN + FP)
(TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)
explanation: Recall is the fraction of actual positives that the model finds. TP/(TP + FP) is precision, the fraction of predicted positives that are correct, which is the most common mix-up.
concept: Recall = TP/(TP + FN); precision = TP/(TP + FP).

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Minimise J(θ) = θ₁² + 3θ₂² by gradient descent from θ = (2, 1) with α = 0.1. What is θ after one update?
explanation: ∇J = (2θ₁, 6θ₂) = (4, 6) at (2, 1), so θ = (2, 1) − 0.1·(4, 6) = (1.6, 0.4). The answer (1.8, 0.7) comes from dropping the factor 2 when differentiating the squares, and (2.4, 1.6) comes from adding the gradient instead of subtracting it.
concept: One GD step: compute ∇J at the current θ, then subtract α times it.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A regression model predicts ŷ = [4, 5, 6, 6] for targets y = [3, 5, 7, 10]. What is the mean squared error (MSE)?
explanation: The residuals are [1, 0, −1, −4], whose squares sum to 18, so MSE = 18/4 = 4.50. The value 1.50 is the MAE (mean absolute error), which grows only linearly with the large fourth residual, and 18 is the sum of squared errors, not its mean.
concept: MSE = mean of squared residuals; squaring makes it sensitive to large errors.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A logistic regression model has θ = (−1, 2, −1) for (intercept, x₁, x₂). For x = (1, 2) with a 0.5 threshold, what are p = σ(θᵀx) and the predicted class (to 3 decimal places)?
options: p = 0.731; class 1
p = 0.269; class 0
p = 0.269; class 1
p = 0.119; class 0
explanation: With the intercept, z = −1 + 2(1) − 1(2) = −1, so p = 1/(1 + e¹) = 0.269 < 0.5 and the prediction is class 0. The value 0.731 is σ(+1), which comes from flipping the sign of z; the sign of z alone already decides the class at a 0.5 threshold.
concept: Under a 0.5 threshold, predict class 1 exactly when θᵀx ≥ 0.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Training points: A(1,1)+, B(2,1)+, C(4,4)−, D(5,4)−, E(3,2)+, F(4,3)−. Using KNN with k = 3 and Euclidean distance, how is the query (3,3) classified?
options: Class + (votes 2 to 1)
Class + (votes 3 to 0)
Class − (votes 3 to 0)
Class − (votes 2 to 1)
explanation: The distances are E = 1, F = 1, C = 1.414, and B = D = 2.236, so the three nearest neighbours are E(+), F(−) and C(−), which gives class − by 2 votes to 1. Class + would need B or A among the three nearest, but both are farther away than C.
concept: KNN: rank by distance, take the k nearest, majority vote.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: For one example with true label y = 1, a classifier outputs p = 0.8. What is its binary cross-entropy (natural log), to 3 decimal places?
explanation: For y = 1 the loss is −ln p = −ln 0.8 = 0.223. The value 1.609 is −ln(1 − p), the loss the example would have if its label were 0, and 0.097 uses base-10 logarithms.
concept: Binary cross-entropy: −[y ln p + (1 − y) ln(1 − p)].

subject: Machine Learning
stem: While running batch gradient descent on a convex MSE loss, you see the loss increase and swing back and forth between iterations, growing each time. What is the most likely cause?
options: The learning rate is too large, so each step overshoots the minimum
The learning rate is too small, so progress stalls
The loss has many local minima that trap the iterates
Too few iterations have been run
explanation: On a convex quadratic, a step that is too large overshoots the minimum, and past a threshold each overshoot is larger than the last, so the loss oscillates and diverges. A learning rate that is too small makes the loss fall slowly but steadily; it never makes it grow.
concept: Rising, oscillating loss in GD signals α above the stability limit.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Of 20 emails, 8 are spam and 12 are ham. The word 'offer' appears in 4 spam emails and 2 ham emails. What is P(spam | 'offer'), to 3 decimal places?
explanation: P(spam | offer) = P(offer | spam)P(spam)/P(offer) = (0.5 × 0.4)/(6/20) = 0.667; equivalently, 4 of the 6 emails containing 'offer' are spam. The value 0.750 compares the two likelihoods but ignores the unequal priors, and 0.500 is the likelihood P(offer | spam), not the posterior.
concept: Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior; both terms matter.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A categorical feature 'colour' has 3 possible values. In class Yes (9 training examples), the value 'red' never occurs. With add-one (Laplace) smoothing, what is P(colour = red | Yes), to 3 decimal places?
explanation: Add-one smoothing gives (count + 1)/(N_class + V) = (0 + 1)/(9 + 3) = 0.083, where V = 3 is the number of feature values. Without smoothing the estimate is 0, which would set the whole class posterior to zero for any red example; adding 1 only to the denominator (giving 0.100) does not produce a valid distribution over the 3 values.
concept: Laplace smoothing: (n_vc + 1)/(n_c + V).

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A linear SVM in canonical form has w = (2, −1) and b = −1. What is the full margin width (the 'street' between the two margin hyperplanes), to 3 decimal places?
explanation: The full width is 2/‖w‖ = 2/√5 = 0.894. The value 0.447 is 1/‖w‖, the half-margin from the boundary to one margin hyperplane, and 0.400 wrongly divides by ‖w‖² instead of ‖w‖.
concept: SVM margin width = 2/‖w‖ under canonical scaling.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A soft-margin SVM has w = (1, 1) and b = −3. For the training point x = (2, 2) with label y = −1, what are the slack ξ = max(0, 1 − y·f(x)) and the point's status?
options: ξ = 0; outside the margin
ξ = 1; on the decision boundary
ξ = 0.5; inside the margin but correctly classified
ξ = 2; misclassified
explanation: f(x) = 2 + 2 − 3 = 1, so y·f = −1 and ξ = 1 − (−1) = 2. Any ξ > 1 means the point is on the wrong side of the boundary; ξ = 0 would require y·f ≥ 1, which fails because the label is −1.
concept: Slack: ξ = 0 outside the margin, 0 < ξ ≤ 1 inside the margin, ξ > 1 misclassified.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Run one iteration of K-means (K = 2) on the 1-D data {2, 4, 5, 10, 12, 15} with initial centroids μ₁ = 2 and μ₂ = 15. What are the updated centroids, to 3 decimal places?
explanation: Assignment puts {2, 4, 5} with μ₁ and {10, 12, 15} with μ₂ (10 is 8 from μ₁ but 5 from μ₂). Averaging gives μ₁ = 11/3 = 3.667 and μ₂ = 37/3 = 12.333. The medians (4 and 12) would be the K-median update, not the K-means mean.
concept: K-means alternates nearest-centroid assignment and mean update.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A classifier's confusion matrix has TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 20, TN = 30. What is its F1 score, to 3 decimal places?
explanation: Precision = 40/50 = 0.800 and recall = 40/60 = 0.667, so F1 = 2PR/(P + R) = 0.727. The value 0.733 is the arithmetic mean of P and R; F1 uses the harmonic mean, which is pulled towards the smaller of the two.
concept: F1 = harmonic mean of precision and recall.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A deep decision tree reaches 99% training accuracy but only 72% validation accuracy. Which diagnosis and remedy fit best?
options: High bias (underfitting): add more features or use a more complex model
Irreducible noise: no change to the model can help
Data leakage: the validation accuracy is inflated and should be ignored
High variance (overfitting): constrain the model (e.g. limit depth or regularise) or add training data
explanation: A large train–validation gap with very low training error is the classic sign of high variance, which simpler models, regularisation or more data reduce. Making the model more complex is the remedy for high bias and would widen this gap further.
concept: A large train–validation gap means high variance.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Fit a no-intercept ridge model y ≈ θx by minimising Σ(yᵢ − θxᵢ)² + λθ² on the data x = [1, 2, 3], y = [2, 4, 7] with λ = 2. What is θ, to 3 decimal places?
explanation: Setting the derivative to zero gives θ = Σxy/(Σx² + λ) = 31/(14 + 2) = 1.938. The value 2.214 is the unregularised OLS estimate; the ridge penalty shrinks θ towards zero, so the ridge value must be smaller than it.
concept: Ridge shrinks coefficients: θ = Σxy/(Σx² + λ) in 1-D.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A test set has 990 negatives and 10 positives. A model predicts 'negative' for every example. Which statement is correct?
options: Accuracy is 0.99 but recall is 0, so the model is useless for finding positives
Accuracy is 0.99 and recall is 0.99, so the model is excellent
Accuracy is 0.01 because no positive is detected
Precision is 1.0 because the model makes no false positives
explanation: The model gets all 990 negatives right, giving 99% accuracy, yet it detects none of the 10 positives, so recall = 0/10 = 0. Precision is undefined (0/0), not 1.0, because the model makes no positive predictions at all; accuracy is misleading under heavy class imbalance.
concept: Under class imbalance, accuracy can hide a useless classifier.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: You train linear regression by batch gradient descent on two features: annual income (around 10⁵) and age (around 10¹). Any α small enough to stop divergence makes progress on the age coefficient extremely slow. What is the best fix?
options: Keep the raw features and shrink α further until the income coefficient is stable
Standardise both features with training-set mean and standard deviation, then rerun GD; the loss contours become rounder, so one α suits both directions
Switch the loss from MSE to MAE so large feature values matter less
Add polynomial terms of age so its coefficient learns faster
explanation: Very different feature scales make the loss surface a long, narrow valley, and the steep income direction caps α, which starves the flat age direction. Standardising equalises the curvature so a single larger α converges quickly; shrinking α avoids divergence but makes the slow direction slower still.
concept: Feature scaling conditions the loss surface and speeds up gradient descent.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A card-fraud model is built on data where 0.5% of transactions are fraud. Missing a fraud costs far more than investigating a false alarm, but analysts can only review a limited number of alerts. Which evaluation approach is most appropriate?
options: Maximise accuracy, because it summarises all four confusion-matrix cells
Use the precision–recall curve (PR-AUC) and pick the threshold that maximises recall at an acceptable precision, on a stratified validation set
Maximise precision alone, because false alarms consume analyst time
Maximise specificity, because negatives dominate the data
explanation: With rare positives, accuracy and specificity are dominated by the easy negatives and barely reflect fraud detection. Recall captures the costly misses, and a precision floor respects the analysts' capacity, so a PR-based threshold choice matches the costs; precision alone would favour flagging very few cases and missing most fraud.
concept: Match the metric and threshold to class imbalance and error costs.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: You have 2,000 labelled examples with 10 numeric features. The classes overlap and the boundary looks curved. Which SVM design and tuning plan is best?
options: Use a hard-margin linear SVM, since the margin maximisation will handle overlap
Use an RBF-SVM with the largest γ that gives zero training error
Standardise in a pipeline, use a soft-margin RBF-SVM, tune C and γ jointly by stratified k-fold cross-validation, then report the score once on a held-out test set
Tune C and γ by checking accuracy on the test set and keep the best pair
explanation: Overlapping classes need a soft margin, a curved boundary suggests a non-linear kernel, and C and γ interact, so they should be searched together by CV on scaled features. A hard margin is infeasible on overlapping data, and tuning on the test set leaks information and gives an optimistic final score.
concept: Soft margin + kernel + joint CV tuning on scaled features; touch the test set once.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Predicting which of five insurance risk groups {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} a customer belongs to is:
options: A regression problem, because the targets are numbers
A clustering problem, because there are five groups
A multi-class classification problem, because the targets are category labels
A binary classification problem, because each customer is either in a group or not
explanation: The task type is set by the target space: a finite set of category codes is classification, and the labels could just as well be A to E. Numeric encoding does not make the target continuous, so treating it as regression (where 2.7 would be a valid output) is the trap.
concept: Task type follows the target space, not the encoding.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: For ordinary least squares with design matrix X (full column rank) and targets y, the closed-form solution is:
options: θ = (XᵀX)Xᵀy
θ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy
θ = (Xᵀy)⁻¹XᵀX
θ = X⁻¹yᵀ
explanation: Setting the gradient of ‖Xθ − y‖² to zero gives the normal equations XᵀXθ = Xᵀy, so θ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy when XᵀX is invertible. The version without the inverse is dimensionally plausible but does not solve the normal equations.
concept: Normal equations: XᵀXθ = Xᵀy.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: In logistic regression, increasing feature x_k by one unit (others fixed) multiplies the odds of y = 1 by:
options: β_k
σ(β_k)
ln(β_k)
e^(β_k)
explanation: The log-odds are linear, so a one-unit increase adds β_k to the log-odds and multiplies the odds by e^(β_k). Reporting β_k itself as the odds ratio forgets to exponentiate; β_k is the change in log-odds.
concept: Odds ratio per unit change = e^β.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: What typically happens when the gradient descent learning rate is set far too large on a convex loss?
options: Convergence becomes slow but stays steady
The algorithm reaches the minimum in exactly one step
The algorithm gets stuck in a local minimum
The iterates overshoot, oscillate and may diverge
explanation: A step that is too large jumps past the minimum, and beyond a stability threshold each jump is larger than the previous one. Slow but steady convergence is the symptom of a learning rate that is too small, and a convex loss has no spurious local minima.
concept: α too large → oscillation/divergence; α too small → slow convergence.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Compared with a larger k, using k = 1 in KNN classification typically gives:
options: High bias and low variance, with a smooth decision boundary
The same boundary as any odd k
Low bias and high variance, with a jagged decision boundary
A linear decision boundary
explanation: With k = 1 every training point, including noisy ones, carves out its own region, so the fit follows the data closely (low bias) but changes a lot with the sample (high variance). Larger k averages over more neighbours and smooths the boundary, which is the high-bias end.
concept: Small k = flexible/high variance; large k = smooth/high bias.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Why is Laplace (add-one) smoothing used in Naive Bayes?
options: To make the features conditionally independent
To stop a single unseen feature value from making a class's posterior exactly zero
To normalise the posteriors so they sum to one
To speed up training on large datasets
explanation: Without smoothing, a feature value never seen with a class gets probability 0, and the product of likelihoods then wipes out all other evidence for that class. Smoothing has nothing to do with the independence assumption; it only avoids zero estimates.
concept: Smoothing prevents zero-frequency likelihoods from vetoing a class.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: In a soft-margin SVM, increasing the penalty C generally:
options: Widens the margin and increases regularisation
Has no effect on the margin, only on training speed
Turns the linear kernel into an RBF kernel
Narrows the margin and reduces regularisation, lowering bias and raising variance
explanation: C multiplies the total slack, so a large C punishes margin violations heavily and the optimiser accepts a narrower margin to fit the training points. Large C therefore means less regularisation, which is the opposite of the 'more regularisation' trap; C behaves like 1/λ.
concept: Large C = less regularisation, narrower margin.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Which formula is the RBF (Gaussian) kernel?
options: k(x, z) = exp(−γ‖x − z‖²)
k(x, z) = (xᵀz + c)^d
k(x, z) = xᵀz
k(x, z) = tanh(γ‖x − z‖)
explanation: The RBF kernel decays with squared Euclidean distance, controlled by γ (γ = 1/(2σ²)). (xᵀz + c)^d is the polynomial kernel and xᵀz is the linear kernel.
concept: RBF kernel: exp(−γ‖x − z‖²), with an infinite-dimensional feature space.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Which statement about the convergence of Lloyd's K-means is correct?
options: It always converges in finitely many steps, but only to a local optimum that depends on initialisation
It always converges to the partition with the globally minimum SSE
It may cycle forever because the SSE can increase
It converges only if the clusters are linearly separable
explanation: Each assignment and update step cannot increase the SSE and there are finitely many partitions, so the algorithm stops, but the stopping point depends on the starting centroids. Exact K-means is NP-hard, which is why K-means++ and multiple restarts are used; global optimality is not guaranteed.
concept: K-means: guaranteed convergence, not guaranteed global optimum.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: The K-means objective (distortion) is:
options: J = Σₙ Σₖ ‖xₙ − μₖ‖, summed over all points and all centroids
J = Σₙ Σₖ r_nk ‖xₙ − μₖ‖², the sum of squared distances to assigned centroids
J = the number of points that change cluster in an iteration
J = the largest distance between any two centroids
explanation: K-means minimises the within-cluster sum of squared Euclidean distances, with r_nk = 1 only for the cluster each point is assigned to. Summing unsquared distances to every centroid ignores the assignments and is a different (and not minimised) quantity.
concept: K-means minimises within-cluster SSE (inertia).

subject: Machine Learning
stem: In k-fold cross-validation, each training example is:
options: Used for validation k times
Used either for training or for validation, never both
Used for validation only if it is misclassified
Used for validation exactly once and for training k − 1 times
explanation: The data are split into k folds and each fold serves once as the validation set while the other k − 1 folds train the model. So every example is validated once and trained on k − 1 times, which makes the CV estimate use all the data.
concept: k-fold CV: k fits, each fold validated once.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Which regulariser tends to set some coefficients exactly to zero, performing feature selection?
options: L2 (ridge), with penalty λΣθⱼ²
Early stopping of gradient descent
L1 (lasso), with penalty λΣ|θⱼ|
Adding more training data
explanation: The L1 penalty has a corner at zero, so the optimum often lands exactly on θⱼ = 0. The L2 penalty shrinks coefficients smoothly towards zero but almost never makes them exactly zero.
concept: L1 → sparse coefficients; L2 → small but non-zero coefficients.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Linear regression ŷ = θ₀ + θ₁x is trained on (x, y) = (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5) with J = (1/2n)Σ(ŷ − y)². Starting at θ = (0, 0) with α = 0.1, what is θ after one batch gradient descent step (3 decimal places)?
explanation: All predictions are 0, so the residuals ŷ − y are (−2, −3, −5). The gradient is ((1/n)Σr, (1/n)Σr·x) = (−3.333, −7.667), and subtracting 0.1 times it gives (0.333, 0.767). The answer (1.000, 2.300) forgets to average over the n = 3 samples.
concept: Batch gradient for MSE: (1/n)Σ(ŷ − y)·x.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A shop records components replaced x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] and repair time y = [3, 5, 6, 8, 11] minutes. Fit ŷ = a + bx by least squares. What are b and a?
explanation: S_xx = 55 − 225/5 = 10 and S_xy = 118 − 15·33/5 = 19, so b = S_xy/S_xx = 1.9 and a = ȳ − b·x̄ = 6.6 − 5.7 = 0.9. A slope of 2.0 uses only the two end points ((11 − 3)/4), which is not the least-squares fit.
concept: Simple least squares: b = S_xy/S_xx, a = ȳ − b·x̄.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A model for death before 60 is log(π/(1 − π)) = −2 + 0.7x, with x = 1 for smokers and 0 for non-smokers. What are the smokers' probability and the odds ratio (smoker vs non-smoker)?
options: π = 0.214; odds ratio = 1.80
π = 0.273; odds ratio = 2.01
π = 0.214; odds ratio = 2.01
π = 0.332; odds ratio = 0.70
explanation: For smokers the log-odds are −1.3, so the odds are e^(−1.3) = 0.273 and π = odds/(1 + odds) = 0.214; the odds ratio is e^0.7 = 2.01. The value 1.80 is the probability (risk) ratio, which is not the same as the odds ratio, and 0.273 is the odds, not the probability.
concept: Odds ratio = e^β; it is not a risk (probability) ratio.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: KNN regression uses training data x = [1, 2, 4, 5, 7] with targets y = [3, 5, 8, 10, 15]. What is the k = 3 prediction for the query x = 4.4 (3 decimal places)?
explanation: The distances from 4.4 are 0.4 (x = 4), 0.6 (x = 5), 2.4 (x = 2) and 2.6 (x = 7), so the three nearest targets are 8, 10 and 5, whose mean is 7.667. The value 9.000 uses only two neighbours, and 8.200 is the mean of all targets, which ignores locality.
concept: KNN regression predicts the mean target of the k nearest neighbours.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Gradient descent on J(θ) = 2θ² uses the update θ ← (1 − 4α)θ. Which learning rate makes the iterates diverge?
explanation: Convergence needs |1 − 4α| < 1, that is 0 < α < 0.5. At α = 0.6 the factor is −1.4, so |θ| grows by 40% each step while alternating in sign. α = 0.45 gives a factor of −0.8, which oscillates but still converges, and α = 0.25 reaches the minimum in one step.
concept: For J = cθ², GD converges iff 0 < α < 1/c.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A fitted logistic regression has coefficient β = −0.4 for 'years since last service'. Holding other features fixed, each additional year multiplies the odds of the positive outcome by about (3 decimal places):
explanation: The odds ratio for a one-unit increase is e^β = e^(−0.4) = 0.670, a reduction of about 33% in the odds. The value 0.401 is σ(β), a probability for a log-odds of −0.4, not a multiplicative effect on the odds.
concept: Negative β → odds ratio below 1.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Training data: 6 'Yes' days and 4 'No' days. Outlook = Sunny on 2 of the Yes days and 3 of the No days; Wind = Strong on 2 of the Yes days and 2 of the No days. For a Sunny, Strong-wind day, what does Naive Bayes predict, and what is the posterior of that class (3 decimal places)?
options: Yes, P(Yes | x) = 0.692
Yes, P(Yes | x) = 0.600
explanation: Score(Yes) = 0.6 × (2/6) × (2/6) = 0.0667 and Score(No) = 0.4 × (3/4) × (2/4) = 0.1500. Normalising gives P(No | x) = 0.1500/0.2167 = 0.692, so the prediction is No. The value 0.150 is the unnormalised score, not a probability, and 0.600 is just the prior for Yes.
concept: NB: multiply prior by per-feature likelihoods, then normalise.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: What is the perpendicular distance of the point (3, 4) from the hyperplane 2x₁ − x₂ − 1 = 0 (3 decimal places)?
explanation: The distance is |wᵀx + b|/‖w‖ = |6 − 4 − 1|/√5 = 1/√5 = 0.447. The value 1.000 is the functional margin |wᵀx + b| without dividing by ‖w‖; since that equals 1, the point lies on a margin hyperplane.
concept: Geometric distance = |wᵀx + b|/‖w‖.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: For x = (1, 2) and z = (3, −1), what is the polynomial kernel value k(x, z) = (xᵀz + 1)²?
explanation: xᵀz = 3 − 2 = 1, so (1 + 1)² = 4. The value 1 is the linear kernel and 0.0015 is the RBF kernel with γ = 0.5; the polynomial kernel adds the constant and then squares.
concept: Polynomial kernel: (xᵀz + c)^d.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: K-means (K = 2) runs on A(1,1), B(1.5,2), C(3,4), D(5,7), E(3.5,5), F(4.5,5), G(3.5,4.5), starting from μ₁ = A and μ₂ = D, with ties going to cluster 1. What is μ₁ after the first update step (3 decimal places)?
explanation: C is at squared distance 13 from both A and D, so the tie rule puts it in cluster 1, giving C₁ = {A, B, C} and μ₁ = (1.833, 2.333). The answer (1.250, 1.500) is the mean of A and B only, which is where μ₁ ends up after the second iteration, or after one iteration if the tie were broken the other way.
concept: State and apply the tie rule; it can change the K-means trajectory.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: K-means++ is run on the points {0, 1, 3, 6, 10} and the first centre chosen is 0. What is the probability that 6 is chosen as the second centre (3 decimal places)?
explanation: K-means++ samples in proportion to D(x)², the squared distance to the nearest chosen centre: D² = 0, 1, 9, 36, 100, which sum to 146, so P(6) = 36/146 = 0.247. The value 0.300 uses unsquared distances, and 0.200 treats all five points as equally likely.
concept: K-means++: P(x) = D(x)²/ΣD².

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A classifier has TP = 30, FN = 10, FP = 20, TN = 140. What are its precision and specificity (3 decimal places)?
options: Precision = 0.600, specificity = 0.875
Precision = 0.750, specificity = 0.875
Precision = 0.600, specificity = 0.933
Precision = 0.875, specificity = 0.600
explanation: Precision = TP/(TP + FP) = 30/50 = 0.600, and specificity = TN/(TN + FP) = 140/160 = 0.875. The value 0.750 is recall (TP/(TP + FN)), and 0.933 is the negative predictive value, which divides by predicted negatives instead of actual negatives.
concept: Specificity = TN/(TN + FP); precision = TP/(TP + FP).

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Learning curves for a linear model show training and validation error both levelling off at about 30% as more data are added, while the target is 5%. What should you do?
options: Collect much more data, since the curves have not converged
Increase model capacity (richer features or a more flexible model); more data alone will not help
Add stronger regularisation to reduce variance
Stop training earlier to avoid overfitting
explanation: Training and validation curves that meet at a high plateau mean high bias: the model cannot represent the pattern even on the training data. More data narrows a gap that is already closed, and extra regularisation or early stopping reduce capacity further, making the bias worse.
concept: Converged-but-high learning curves = high bias → add capacity.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: You run 5-fold cross-validation on 1,000 examples. How many models are trained, and how many examples does each one train on?
options: 5 models, each trained on 800 examples
5 models, each trained on 200 examples
1 model trained on 1,000 examples, validated 5 times
4 models, each trained on 750 examples
explanation: Each of the 5 folds (200 examples) is held out once while the model trains on the remaining 4 folds, so 5 models each train on 800 examples. Training on 200 confuses the validation fold with the training set.
concept: k-fold CV trains k models on (k − 1)/k of the data.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Ridge regression gives training MSE 2.1, 2.3, 2.9, 6.5 and validation MSE 7.8, 4.1, 3.6, 6.9 for λ = 0, 0.1, 1, 10 respectively. Which λ should you choose, and why?
options: λ = 0, because it gives the lowest training MSE
λ = 10, because the strongest penalty generalises best
λ = 0.1, because it balances the training and validation MSE most evenly
λ = 1, because it gives the lowest validation MSE
explanation: Hyperparameters are chosen on validation error, which is U-shaped in λ and lowest (3.6) at λ = 1. λ = 0 fits training data best but overfits (validation 7.8), while λ = 10 over-shrinks and underfits (both errors high).
concept: Choose λ at the minimum of validation error, not training error.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A KNN credit model uses age (20–70 years) and annual income (₹2,00,000–₹50,00,000) with raw Euclidean distance, and its neighbours are effectively matched on income alone. What is the best fix?
options: Increase k until age begins to matter
Switch to Manhattan distance on the raw features
Standardise (or min–max scale) both features using training-set statistics, then choose k by cross-validation
Drop age, since it does not affect the distance anyway
explanation: Income's range is about 10⁵ times larger than age's, so it dominates any raw Minkowski distance, Manhattan included. Scaling puts the features on comparable ranges so both contribute; changing k or the distance type leaves the scale imbalance untouched.
concept: Distance-based methods need feature scaling.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: An engineer copies the binary feature 'contains free' into five identical columns before training a Naive Bayes spam filter. What is the most accurate assessment?
options: The same evidence is multiplied in five times, violating conditional independence and pushing posteriors towards overconfident extremes
Nothing changes, because Naive Bayes ignores duplicated features
Accuracy must improve, because the model has more features
The posteriors become better calibrated, because the evidence is reinforced
explanation: Naive Bayes multiplies one likelihood ratio per feature, so five copies raise that word's evidence to the fifth power, as if they were five independent clues. The ranking of emails may change little, but probabilities become overconfident; Naive Bayes has no mechanism to detect duplicates.
concept: Correlated features double-count evidence in Naive Bayes.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Your 2-D data form two concentric rings. K-means with K = 2 splits them into left and right halves instead. What is the best response?
options: Increase n_init so K-means finds the global optimum
Standardise the features and rerun K-means
Use a method that does not assume compact convex clusters, such as spectral clustering or DBSCAN, or cluster on a transformed feature such as the radius
Choose K by the minimum SSE and rerun
explanation: K-means assigns points to the nearest centroid, so its clusters are convex (Voronoi) regions, and no centroid placement can separate one ring from another. More restarts only find better convex splits, and choosing K by minimum SSE always favours more clusters without fixing the shape problem.
concept: K-means assumes compact, roughly spherical clusters.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A classifier achieves zero training error. What can you conclude about its test error?
options: It will have the lowest test error of any model
Its test error will also be zero
Nothing definite; it must be measured on held-out data, and zero training error may indicate overfitting
Its test error will equal its validation error
explanation: Training error measures fit to data the model has already seen, while generalisation is judged on unseen data. A high-capacity model can memorise noise and reach zero training error yet do worse on test data than a simpler model.
concept: Judge models by held-out error, not training error.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: You add a feature x₃ = 2x₁ to a linear regression design matrix. What happens to the OLS solution?
options: XᵀX becomes singular, so there is no unique θ; drop the column, use the pseudo-inverse, or add ridge
θ becomes unique and more accurate
Training MSE rises sharply
Only the intercept changes
explanation: An exact multiple of an existing column makes the columns linearly dependent, so XᵀX is not invertible and infinitely many θ give the same fit. The fit itself (the training MSE) does not change; only the uniqueness of the coefficients is lost.
concept: Perfect collinearity → singular XᵀX → no unique OLS solution.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: What is the range of the logistic sigmoid σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^(−z)) for real z?
options: The closed interval [−1, 1]
All real numbers
The open interval (0, 1)
The set {0, 1}
explanation: As z → −∞, σ(z) → 0, and as z → +∞, σ(z) → 1, but it never reaches either value; σ(0) = 0.5. The interval (−1, 1) is the range of tanh, a different squashing function.
concept: σ maps any real score to a probability in (0, 1).

subject: Machine Learning
stem: How does stochastic gradient descent (SGD) differ from batch gradient descent?
options: SGD computes the exact full-data gradient at every step
SGD updates θ using the gradient from one sample (or a small mini-batch) at a time, giving cheaper but noisier steps
SGD needs no learning rate
SGD solves the normal equations in closed form
explanation: Batch GD averages the gradient over all n samples before each update, while SGD uses one sample (or a mini-batch), so each step costs far less but follows a noisier path. SGD still needs a learning rate and is still iterative.
concept: SGD trades gradient accuracy for cheap, frequent updates.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Which of these is a hyperparameter of a KNN classifier?
options: The weight vector learned by gradient descent
The number of neighbours k
The intercept term θ₀
The learning rate α
explanation: KNN has no trained weights; its behaviour is set by choices such as k, the distance metric and the neighbour weighting. Weight vectors, intercepts and learning rates belong to parametric models trained by optimisation.
concept: KNN is non-parametric; k and the metric are its main hyperparameters.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: How does Gaussian Naive Bayes handle a continuous feature?
options: It fits a normal distribution to the feature separately for each class and uses its density as P(x_j | y)
It discretises the feature into equal-width bins
It fits one normal distribution to the feature across all classes
It ignores continuous features
explanation: Gaussian NB estimates a class-specific mean and variance for each feature and plugs the normal density into the Naive Bayes product. A single distribution pooled across classes would give the same likelihood for every class and so carry no class information.
concept: Gaussian NB: class-conditional normal densities per feature.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: In a trained hard-margin SVM, you delete a training point that lies strictly outside the margin. What happens to the decision boundary?
options: Nothing; the point has α = 0 and does not contribute to w or b
It shifts towards the deleted point
It must be retrained and will generally change
The margin widens by the point's distance
explanation: Only support vectors have non-zero dual coefficients, and w = Σαᵢyᵢxᵢ, so a point with α = 0 contributes nothing. Retraining without it returns the same solution, which is the sparsity property of SVMs.
concept: SVM solutions depend only on the support vectors.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: What does the 'kernel trick' allow an SVM to do?
options: Train without any labelled data
Turn a non-convex problem into a convex one
Output calibrated class probabilities
Compute inner products in a high-dimensional feature space without constructing the feature vectors explicitly
explanation: The dual problem and the prediction use the data only through inner products, so replacing xᵢᵀxⱼ with k(xᵢ, xⱼ) = φ(xᵢ)ᵀφ(xⱼ) works in feature space at the cost of a kernel evaluation. The SVM problem is already convex, and kernels do not produce probabilities.
concept: Kernel trick: k(x, z) = φ(x)ᵀφ(z) without computing φ.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Why can you not choose the number of clusters K by picking the value with the smallest SSE?
options: SSE is undefined for K greater than 2
The optimal SSE never increases with K and reaches 0 when K = N, so it always favours more clusters
SSE increases with K, so it would always pick K = 1
SSE depends only on the initialisation, not on K
explanation: Adding a cluster can never make the best achievable SSE worse, and with one cluster per point the SSE is 0; that is the clustering version of zero training error. Use the elbow method, silhouette scores or domain knowledge instead.
concept: Choose K by elbow/silhouette, never by minimum SSE.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Standardising every feature, z = (x − μ)/σ, before running K-means:
options: Never changes the clusters, because the shapes are preserved
Only changes the number of iterations, not the result
Is required for K-means to converge
Can change the clusters found, because Euclidean distance is not scale-invariant
explanation: Rescaling a feature changes which centroid is nearest to each point, so assignments and clusters can change. This contrasts with unregularised OLS, whose predictions are unchanged by standardisation; K-means converges either way.
concept: Distance-based clustering is sensitive to feature scale.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A ROC curve plots:
options: Precision against recall at a fixed threshold
Training error against validation error as model size grows
Accuracy against the number of training examples
True positive rate against false positive rate as the decision threshold varies
explanation: Each threshold gives a (FPR, TPR) pair, and sweeping the threshold traces the ROC curve; the area under it (AUC) summarises ranking quality. Precision against recall is the PR curve, which is more informative when positives are rare.
concept: ROC: TPR vs FPR across thresholds.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: For squared-error loss, the expected test error at a point decomposes as:
options: Bias² + variance + irreducible noise
Bias + variance
Bias² − variance + noise
Training error + validation error
explanation: Averaging over training sets, E[(y − ŷ)²] = (E[ŷ] − f)² + Var(ŷ) + σ², where σ² is noise no model can remove. Bias enters squared, so 'bias + variance' has the wrong form and leaves out the noise term.
concept: Expected MSE = bias² + variance + σ².

subject: Machine Learning
stem: For J(θ₀, θ₁) = ½[(2θ₁ − 2)² + (θ₀ − 3)²], take one gradient descent step from θ = (0, 0) with α = 0.25. What is the new θ?
explanation: ∇J = (θ₀ − 3, 4θ₁ − 4) = (−3, −4) at the origin, so θ = (0, 0) − 0.25·(−3, −4) = (0.75, 1.00). The answer (0.75, 0.50) drops the chain-rule factor 2 from (2θ₁ − 2)², and (3, 1) is the minimiser, which one step does not reach.
concept: Apply the chain rule carefully when forming ∇J.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: The least-squares line ŷ = 0.9 + 1.9x is fitted to x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], y = [3, 5, 6, 8, 11]. What is R² (3 decimal places)?
explanation: SSE = 1.10 and SST = Σ(y − ȳ)² = 37.2, so R² = 1 − SSE/SST = 0.970. The value 0.030 is the unexplained fraction SSE/SST, and 0.985 is the correlation r = √R² for simple regression.
concept: R² = 1 − SSE/SST.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A logistic model has z = −1 + 1.5x₁ − 0.5x₂. For the samples A(1, 2; y = 1), B(2, 1; y = 1) and C(0, 1; y = 0), what is the mean binary cross-entropy (natural log, 3 decimal places)?
explanation: z = (−0.5, 1.5, −1.5) gives p = (0.378, 0.818, 0.182), and the per-sample losses are −ln p, −ln p and −ln(1 − p) = (0.974, 0.201, 0.201), whose mean is 0.459. The value 0.974 is the loss of the misclassified sample A alone, and 1.377 is the sum rather than the mean.
concept: Mean BCE averages −[y ln p + (1 − y) ln(1 − p)] over samples.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: The query is (0, 0). Training point P = (3, 0) has class A and Q = (2, 2) has class B. What does 1-NN predict under Euclidean and under Manhattan distance?
options: Euclidean: A; Manhattan: B
Both predict A
Euclidean: B; Manhattan: A
Both predict B
explanation: Euclidean distances are 3 to P and √8 = 2.828 to Q, so Q (class B) is nearer. Manhattan distances are 3 to P and 4 to Q, so P (class A) is nearer. The distance metric is a real modelling choice that can flip KNN predictions.
concept: The choice of distance metric changes KNN's neighbours.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: For a query, the 3 nearest neighbours are at distances 1 (class +), 2 (class −) and 2.5 (class −). What are the predictions of plain majority-vote 3-NN and of 3-NN weighted by 1/distance?
options: Majority vote: +; distance-weighted: −
Both predict −
Both predict +
Majority vote: −; distance-weighted: +
explanation: The plain vote is 2 to 1 for −. With 1/d weights, + gets 1/1 = 1.0 and − gets 1/2 + 1/2.5 = 0.9, so + wins. Weighting lets a very close neighbour outvote several farther ones.
concept: Distance weighting gives closer neighbours more say.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A model predicts probability p = 0.8 for the positive class. What is the log-odds (logit) ln(p/(1 − p)), to 3 decimal places?
explanation: The odds are 0.8/0.2 = 4, so the log-odds are ln 4 = 1.386. The value 4.000 is the odds before taking the logarithm, and −0.223 is ln p, which leaves out the (1 − p) denominator.
concept: logit(p) = ln(p/(1 − p)); odds = p/(1 − p).

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A disease has 1% prevalence. A test has 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity. What is P(disease | positive test), to 3 decimal places?
explanation: By Bayes' theorem, P(D | +) = (0.9 × 0.01)/(0.9 × 0.01 + 0.05 × 0.99) = 0.009/0.0585 = 0.154. The value 0.900 is the sensitivity P(+ | D), the classic mistake of inverting the conditional and ignoring the low prior.
concept: Low priors keep posteriors low even for accurate tests.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: In multinomial Naive Bayes, the spam class contains 20 word tokens in total, the vocabulary has 10 words, and 'win' occurs 3 times in spam. With add-one smoothing, what is P('win' | spam), to 3 decimal places?
explanation: Add-one smoothing gives (count + 1)/(total tokens + V) = (3 + 1)/(20 + 10) = 0.133. The value 0.150 is the unsmoothed estimate, and 0.200 adds 1 to the count without adding V to the denominator, so the probabilities would no longer sum to 1.
concept: Multinomial NB smoothing: (n_w + 1)/(N + V).

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A hard-margin SVM is trained on class +1 points (3, 1) and (3, −1) and the class −1 point (1, 0). What is the full margin width?
explanation: By symmetry the boundary is x₁ = 2. The canonical constraints give w = (1, 0) and b = −2, so the width is 2/‖w‖ = 2, which matches the gap between x₁ = 1 and x₁ = 3. The value 1 is the half-margin 1/‖w‖.
concept: Find w, b from canonical constraints on the support vectors; width = 2/‖w‖.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: For a hard-margin SVM, the KKT conditions imply ‖w‖² = Σᵢαᵢ. If the optimal dual coefficients sum to 4, what is the full margin width?
explanation: ‖w‖ = √(Σα) = √4 = 2, so the width is 2/‖w‖ = 1. The value 0.5 is the half-margin 1/‖w‖, and 0.25 is 1/Σα, which wrongly uses ‖w‖² in place of ‖w‖.
concept: Hard-margin identity: ‖w‖² = Σαᵢ, so width = 2/√Σαᵢ.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: For the clustering {1, 2, 3} and {8, 9} on a number line, what is the silhouette value of the point 3 (3 decimal places)?
explanation: a = mean distance to its own cluster = (2 + 1)/2 = 1.5, and b = mean distance to the other cluster = (5 + 6)/2 = 5.5, so s = (b − a)/max(a, b) = 0.727. The value 0.800 uses nearest-point distances instead of mean distances, and 0.273 is a/b, which is 1 − s.
concept: Silhouette s = (b − a)/max(a, b), in [−1, 1].

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Lloyd's K-means (K = 2) runs on {1, 2, 3, 4} from initial centres {2, 4}, with ties going to the lower-index cluster. At what SSE does it stop, and what is the optimal SSE?
options: Stops at J = 2; optimal J = 1
Stops at J = 1; optimal J = 1
Stops at J = 2; optimal J = 0.5
Stops at J = 4; optimal J = 1
explanation: Point 3 ties and joins cluster 1, giving {1, 2, 3} with mean 2 and {4} with mean 4. No assignment then changes, so it stops at J = 1 + 0 + 1 + 0 = 2. The partition {1, 2}, {3, 4} has J = 4 × 0.25 = 1, so Lloyd's algorithm can stop at twice the optimum.
concept: Lloyd's algorithm can stop at a poor fixed point; use restarts or K-means++.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A fraud model flags 50 transactions, of which 35 are truly fraudulent. The data contain 70 fraudulent transactions in total. What is the F1 score (3 decimal places)?
explanation: Precision = 35/50 = 0.700 and recall = 35/70 = 0.500, so F1 = 2PR/(P + R) = 0.583. The arithmetic mean 0.600 overstates performance; the harmonic mean is pulled towards the weaker of the two.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: At a test point the true value is f(x₀) = 10. Models trained on four different training sets predict 8, 9, 11 and 12. Using the population variance, what are bias² and variance?
options: Bias² = 2.5, variance = 0.0
Bias² = 0.0, variance = 3.333
Bias² = 1.0, variance = 2.5
Bias² = 0.0, variance = 2.5
explanation: The mean prediction is 10, which equals the truth, so bias² = 0. The variance is the mean of the squared deviations (4 + 1 + 1 + 4)/4 = 2.5. The value 3.333 divides by n − 1, the sample variance, which the stem rules out.
concept: Bias = average prediction − truth; variance = spread of predictions across training sets.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A team standardises the full dataset (computing mean and standard deviation on all rows) and then runs 5-fold cross-validation. What is the problem, and what is the fix?
options: There is no problem, because standardisation is unsupervised
The CV estimate will be too pessimistic; scale after training instead
Statistics from the validation folds leak into training, biasing the CV estimate; fit the scaler inside each training fold with a pipeline
Standardisation makes k-fold invalid; use a single train–test split instead
explanation: Any preprocessing fitted on data includes the held-out fold's information, so validation no longer imitates truly unseen data and estimates become optimistic. Fitting the transformer on each training fold only, as a pipeline does automatically, removes the leak; being unsupervised does not make it leak-free.
concept: Fit all preprocessing inside the CV loop to avoid leakage.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A quadratic model ŷ = θ₀ + θ₁x + θ₂x² fitted to exactly three training points reaches training MSE = 0. A colleague says it will therefore generalise well. What is the best assessment?
options: Agree: zero training error proves the model is correct
Agree, as long as the points are exact rather than noisy measurements
Disagree, because a quadratic can never fit three points exactly
Disagree: with 3 parameters and 3 points the model interpolates, so zero training error says nothing about generalisation; estimate error on held-out data or by CV
explanation: With as many parameters as data points, the system is solved exactly, so any three points, noise included, give zero training error. Only held-out or cross-validated error reveals generalisation; and a quadratic can always pass through three points with distinct x, so the last option is false.
concept: Interpolation (parameters ≥ points) gives zero training error regardless of truth.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A bank needs a classifier whose outputs can be used directly as default probabilities for pricing loans. Which choice is most defensible?
options: Logistic regression (regularised and checked for calibration on validation data), since it models P(y | x) through the log-loss
A kernel SVM, using the raw decision values f(x) as probabilities
A kernel SVM, min–max scaling the decision values to [0, 1]
KNN with k = 1, using the neighbour's label as the probability
explanation: Pricing needs calibrated probabilities, and logistic regression is fitted by maximum likelihood on exactly that quantity. SVM decision values are unbounded scores, and rescaling them to [0, 1] does not calibrate them; that requires a separate fit such as Platt scaling on held-out data.
concept: When probabilities matter, use a probabilistic model or explicit calibration.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: You must estimate the performance of a model that forecasts next week's sales from the past three years of weekly data. Which validation design is best?
options: Shuffled 10-fold cross-validation over all weeks
Forward-chaining (rolling-origin) splits: train on earlier weeks, validate on the weeks that follow, and repeat, never training on the future
Leave-one-out cross-validation over randomly ordered weeks
A random 80/20 split, repeated five times
explanation: Time series are autocorrelated, and deployment always predicts the future from the past. Shuffled splits let the model train on weeks after the ones it is validated on, which leaks future information and inflates the score; rolling-origin evaluation imitates real deployment.
concept: Validation splits must respect the time order of the data.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A linear regression model with an intercept uses 10 input features. What is the dimension of its parameter space Θ?
options: ℝ¹⁰
ℝ²⁰
ℝ¹¹
ℝ¹
explanation: There is one weight per feature plus the intercept θ₀, giving 10 + 1 = 11 parameters. Writing ℝ¹⁰ forgets the intercept, which is the most common slip.
concept: A linear model with d features and an intercept has d + 1 parameters.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A single large outlier is added to a regression training set. Which fitted line is pulled more strongly towards it?
options: The line trained with MAE, because absolute values amplify large residuals
The line trained with MSE, because squaring makes the outlier's loss and gradient grow with its residual
Both are pulled equally, because both losses are minimised
Neither, because least squares ignores outliers
explanation: A residual of 10 contributes 100 to the squared-error sum but only 10 to the absolute-error sum, and the MSE gradient grows with the residual while the MAE gradient stays at ±1. MSE is therefore pulled more, and MAE is the more robust loss.
concept: MSE is sensitive to outliers; MAE is more robust.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Logistic regression is linear in which quantity?
options: The probability p
The log-odds, ln(p/(1 − p))
The odds p/(1 − p)
The class label y
explanation: Logistic regression sets ln(p/(1 − p)) = θᵀx, so the log-odds are linear in x and θ. The probability itself is an S-shaped function of θᵀx, and the odds are exponential in it.
concept: Logistic regression: logit(p) = θᵀx.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Why does standardising features usually speed up gradient descent?
options: It makes the loss contours rounder, so a single learning rate suits every parameter direction
It reduces the number of parameters
It makes the loss function convex
It removes the need for a learning rate
explanation: Very different feature scales give a long, narrow loss valley; the steep direction limits α while the shallow one converges slowly. Standardising evens out the curvature. It does not change the number of parameters, and the MSE of linear regression is convex either way.
concept: Feature scaling improves the conditioning of gradient descent.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Why does KNN tend to degrade when the number of features becomes very large?
options: In high dimensions, distances between points become similar, so the 'nearest' neighbours are barely nearer than the rest
KNN cannot compute distances for more than three features
More features always reduce the training error to zero
The value of k must equal the number of features
explanation: As the dimension grows, the ratio between the nearest and farthest distances approaches 1 and data become sparse, so neighbourhoods stop being local or informative. This is the curse of dimensionality; distances can still be computed, they just lose discriminating power.
concept: Curse of dimensionality: distance contrast collapses in high dimensions.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Naive Bayes is a generative classifier. This means it:
options: Directly models P(y | x) without modelling the features
Generates new training data to augment the dataset
Models P(x | y) and P(y), then uses Bayes' rule to obtain P(y | x)
Learns a decision boundary by maximising the margin
explanation: A generative model describes how features arise in each class, P(x | y), together with the class priors, and inverts them with Bayes' rule. Directly modelling P(y | x), as logistic regression does, is the discriminative approach.
concept: Generative: model P(x | y)P(y); discriminative: model P(y | x).

subject: Machine Learning
stem: In a soft-margin SVM, a training point with slack ξᵢ > 1 is:
options: Correctly classified and outside the margin
Exactly on the margin
Inside the margin but correctly classified
Misclassified, on the wrong side of the decision boundary
explanation: ξ = max(0, 1 − y·f), so ξ > 1 means y·f < 0, which is the wrong side of the boundary. Points inside the margin but correctly classified have 0 < ξ ≤ 1.
concept: ξ > 1 ⇔ misclassified.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: An SVM with an RBF kernel has a curved decision boundary in input space. Which statement is correct?
options: It is still linear in its parameters (w or α); the boundary is a hyperplane in feature space
It is non-linear in w, so the optimisation is non-convex
It cannot be called linear in any sense
It is equivalent to logistic regression on the raw inputs
explanation: f(x) = wᵀφ(x) + b = Σαᵢyᵢk(xᵢ, x) + b is linear in w and α, and the training problem remains a convex QP. The curvature appears only when the feature-space hyperplane is viewed back in x-space, the same distinction as polynomial regression being linear in θ.
concept: Kernel SVMs are linear in parameters, non-linear in inputs.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: In K-means++ initialisation, after the first centre is chosen, each next centre is picked:
options: As the point farthest from all chosen centres, deterministically
Uniformly at random from all points
As the mean of all points
At random with probability proportional to D(x)², the squared distance to the nearest centre already chosen
explanation: D² sampling spreads the centres out while staying random, which gives a provable bound on the expected SSE. Always picking the farthest point is deterministic and very sensitive to outliers.
concept: K-means++: sample the next centre with probability ∝ D(x)².

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Your data contain a few extreme outliers that drag K-means centroids away from the dense groups. Which alternative is more robust?
options: K-medoids, which uses actual data points as centres
K-means with more iterations
K-means with a larger K and no other change
K-means++ initialisation alone
explanation: The mean minimises squared distances, so one far-away point shifts it a lot. A medoid must be a data point and minimises total dissimilarity, so it moves much less. Better initialisation or more iterations do not change what the mean optimises.
concept: Outliers distort means; medoids are more robust.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Raising a binary classifier's decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.8 typically:
options: Increases or keeps precision and lowers or keeps recall
Increases both precision and recall
Lowers precision and raises recall
Leaves precision and recall unchanged
explanation: A higher threshold labels fewer examples positive, so the positives it keeps are usually more reliable (precision tends to rise) and some true positives are lost (recall cannot rise). Lowering the threshold has the opposite effect.
concept: Threshold controls the precision–recall trade-off.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: The ridge regression penalty added to the squared-error loss is:
options: λΣⱼ|θⱼ|
λ times the number of non-zero coefficients
λΣⱼθⱼ², usually excluding the intercept
λΣᵢ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²
explanation: Ridge (L2) penalises the squared size of the coefficients, shrinking them towards zero; the intercept is normally left unpenalised. λΣ|θⱼ| is the lasso (L1) penalty, and the last option just rescales the data loss.
concept: Ridge = L2 penalty λ‖θ‖².

subject: Machine Learning
stem: An SGD step for ŷ = θ₀ + θ₁x uses the per-sample loss ½(ŷ − y)². With θ = (1, 1), the sample (x = 2, y = 6) and α = 0.1, what is the updated θ?
explanation: ŷ = 3, so the error ŷ − y = −3 and the gradient is (−3, −3·2) = (−3, −6). θ − 0.1·(−3, −6) = (1.3, 1.6). The answer (1.3, 1.3) forgets to multiply the θ₁ component by x, and (1.6, 2.2) doubles the gradient, which the ½ in the loss cancels.
concept: Per-sample (LMS) gradient: (ŷ − y)·x̃.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Fit ŷ = θ₀ + θ₁x + θ₂x² exactly to the points (−1, 2), (0, 1) and (1, 4). What is (θ₀, θ₁, θ₂)?
explanation: The row for x = 0 gives θ₀ = 1. Subtracting the x = −1 row from the x = 1 row gives 2θ₁ = 2, so θ₁ = 1, and then the x = −1 row gives θ₂ = 2. Check: 1 + x + 2x² gives 2, 1 and 4. (1, −1, 2) has the wrong sign on θ₁: it fits x = −1 with a value of 4 instead of 2.
concept: With a basis expansion, solve Xθ = y using design-matrix rows [1, x, x²].

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A logistic model with z = −1 + 1.5x₁ − 0.5x₂ is applied to A(1, 2), B(2, 1) and C(0, 1). If the decision threshold is lowered to 0.3, which samples are predicted positive?
options: B only
A, B and C
A and B
A only
explanation: z = (−0.5, 1.5, −1.5) gives p = (0.378, 0.818, 0.182). At a 0.3 threshold, A (0.378) and B (0.818) are positive but C (0.182) is not. 'B only' is the answer at the default 0.5 threshold.
concept: Changing the threshold changes predictions without changing the model.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: On a number line the labelled points are 1(A), 2(A), 3(B), 4(A), 5(B), 6(B), 7(B). What do 1-NN and 3-NN predict for the query 3.4?
options: 1-NN: B; 3-NN: A
1-NN: A; 3-NN: B
1-NN: B; 3-NN: B
1-NN: A; 3-NN: A
explanation: The nearest points are 3 (B, distance 0.4), 4 (A, 0.6) and 2 (A, 1.4). 1-NN takes only point 3 and predicts B, while 3-NN votes B, A, A and predicts A. Taking more neighbours can override the single closest point.
concept: Different k can flip the KNN prediction.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Two negative examples (y = 0) receive predicted probabilities p = 0.99 and p = 0.6 of being positive. What are their binary cross-entropy losses (natural log, 3 decimal places)?
explanation: For y = 0 the loss is −ln(1 − p): −ln 0.01 = 4.605 and −ln 0.4 = 0.916. The confidently wrong prediction is penalised about five times more, which is how log-loss punishes overconfidence. Using −ln p, as for y = 1, gives the wrong pair.
concept: Log-loss heavily penalises confident mistakes.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: In an OLS model, house price has coefficient 2.5 per metre of frontage. If frontage is re-expressed in centimetres and the model is refitted, what happens?
options: The coefficient becomes 250 per cm and the predictions are unchanged
The coefficient becomes 0.025 per cm and the predictions are unchanged
The coefficient stays 2.5 and the predictions are multiplied by 100
The coefficient becomes 0.025 and the training MSE falls
explanation: Multiplying a feature by 100 divides its OLS coefficient by 100, so 2.5 × (1/100) = 0.025 per cm, and θx is unchanged. Predictions and MSE stay the same because the hypothesis space is identical; multiplying the coefficient by 100 instead gets the direction of the rescaling backwards.
concept: OLS predictions are invariant to linear rescaling of features.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: There are 5 'Buy = yes' and 5 'Buy = no' customers. P(young | yes) = 1/5, P(young | no) = 3/5; P(high income | yes) = 2/5, P(high income | no) = 4/5; P(student | yes) = 4/5, P(student | no) = 1/5. For a young, high-income student, what does Naive Bayes give?
options: Predict yes; P(yes | x) = 0.600
Predict no; P(yes | x) = 0.032
Predict yes; P(yes | x) = 0.500
Predict no; P(yes | x) = 0.400
explanation: Score(yes) = 0.5 × 0.2 × 0.4 × 0.8 = 0.032 and score(no) = 0.5 × 0.6 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.048. So P(yes | x) = 0.032/0.080 = 0.400 and the prediction is no. The value 0.032 is the unnormalised score, not a posterior probability.
concept: Normalise NB scores across classes to get posteriors.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Gaussian Naive Bayes with one feature: class A has μ = 1, σ = 1 and class B has μ = 4, σ = 2, with equal priors. For x = 2, which class is predicted, and what is its posterior (3 decimal places)?
options: Class B, posterior 0.667
Class A, posterior 0.667
Class A, posterior 0.500
Class B, posterior 0.500
explanation: Both z-scores are 1, but the normal density is divided by σ, so p(x | A) = 0.2420 and p(x | B) = 0.1210, which is half as large. With equal priors, P(A | x) = 0.667. Treating equal z-scores as equal likelihoods (posterior 0.5) ignores the 1/σ factor.
concept: Gaussian likelihood depends on σ as well as on the z-score.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A canonical linear SVM has w = (2, −1) and b = −1. Which point lies exactly on a margin hyperplane (|wᵀx + b| = 1)?
explanation: f(3, 4) = 6 − 4 − 1 = 1, so it is on the +1 margin and is a potential support vector. f(1, 1) = 0 lies on the decision boundary, not on a margin, while (2, 1) and (0, 1) give f = 2 and −2, which are outside the margin.
concept: Margin hyperplanes: wᵀx + b = ±1; boundary: wᵀx + b = 0.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Three training points have margins y·f(x) = 2, 0.5 and −1. What is their total hinge loss Σmax(0, 1 − y·f)?
explanation: The losses are max(0, −1) = 0, max(0, 0.5) = 0.5 and max(0, 2) = 2, giving 2.5. Dropping the max lets the well-classified point contribute −1, which gives 1.5; points beyond the margin should add nothing.
concept: Hinge loss is zero for points with y·f ≥ 1.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: The points (1,1), (2,1), (4,3) and (5,4) are assigned to the nearest of the centroids (1.5, 1) and (4.5, 3.5). What is the K-means objective J (sum of squared distances)?
explanation: The squared distances are 0.25, 0.25, 0.5 and 0.5, so J = 1.500. The value 2.414 adds unsquared Euclidean distances, but the K-means objective uses squared distances.
concept: J sums squared distances to the assigned centroids.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: The best SSE for K = 1 to 6 is 600, 210, 95, 80, 70 and 62. Using the elbow method, which K should you choose?
explanation: The percentage drops are 65.0, 54.8, 15.8, 12.5, 11.4. They are large up to K = 3 and small after it, so the curve bends at K = 3. K = 6 has the lowest SSE, but SSE always falls as K grows, so minimum SSE is not a valid criterion.
concept: Elbow: pick K where extra clusters stop reducing SSE substantially.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: A screening model has TP = 8, FN = 2, TN = 900, FP = 90. What is its balanced accuracy, the mean of recall and specificity (3 decimal places)?
explanation: Recall = 8/10 = 0.800 and specificity = 900/990 = 0.909, so balanced accuracy = 0.855. Plain accuracy (0.908) is dominated by the 990 negatives, and precision is only 0.082 because most alarms are false.
concept: Balanced accuracy averages per-class recall, resisting class imbalance.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Polynomial models of degree 1, 3, 6 and 12 give training MSE 9.8, 3.1, 2.7, 0.2 and validation MSE 10.1, 3.4, 4.0, 15.7. Which reading is correct?
options: Degree 12 is best because its training MSE is lowest
Degree 1 underfits, degree 12 overfits, and degree 3 should be chosen
Degree 1 overfits because its errors are similar
Degree 6 is best because it lies between the extremes
explanation: Degree 1 has high error on both sets (high bias). Degree 12 has tiny training error but huge validation error (high variance). Validation MSE is lowest at degree 3, so that is the model to choose; the lowest training MSE is the overfitting trap.
concept: Pick model complexity at the minimum of validation error.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: As λ increases, model P's coefficient for feature 7 goes 0.82 → 0.41 → 0.00 → 0.00, while model Q's goes 0.82 → 0.55 → 0.21 → 0.06. Which is the most likely pairing?
options: P is lasso (L1) and Q is ridge (L2)
P is ridge (L2) and Q is lasso (L1)
Both are ridge with different learning rates
Both are unregularised OLS
explanation: The L1 penalty drives coefficients exactly to zero at a finite λ and keeps them there, which is P's pattern. The L2 penalty shrinks coefficients smoothly towards zero without reaching it, as in Q. OLS has no λ at all.
concept: L1 paths hit zero; L2 paths approach zero asymptotically.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Unregularised logistic regression is trained by gradient descent on perfectly linearly separable data. The weights keep growing and never converge. What is the best explanation and fix?
options: The learning rate is too small; increase it until the weights converge
The sigmoid is non-convex, so gradient descent is trapped; use random restarts
The data must be standardised; then a finite maximum-likelihood solution always exists
The likelihood keeps improving as ‖θ‖ → ∞ along the separating direction, so no finite optimum exists; add L2 regularisation (or stop early)
explanation: On separable data, scaling θ up pushes every σ(θᵀx) towards the correct 0 or 1, so the log-loss approaches 0 but never reaches a minimum. A penalty λ‖θ‖² restores a finite, unique optimum. The log-loss is convex, so restarts do not help, and scaling the data does not remove separability.
concept: Separable data → unregularised logistic MLE diverges; regularise.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: You have n = 200 samples and p = 5,000 features, and domain experts believe only a handful of features matter. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Ordinary least squares on all 5,000 features
Lasso (L1) regression with λ chosen by cross-validation, giving a sparse, interpretable model
Ridge regression, keeping all 5,000 features with small coefficients
KNN on all 5,000 raw features
explanation: With p ≫ n, XᵀX is singular, so OLS has no unique solution. Lasso both regularises and selects a sparse subset, which matches the belief that few features matter. Ridge would also stabilise the fit but keeps every feature, and KNN suffers badly from the curse of dimensionality here.
concept: Use L1 when p ≫ n and the true signal is sparse.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: You must segment customers using annual spend (₹), visit count and a categorical 'preferred channel' (store/online/app). Which plan is best?
options: Run K-means on the raw features with K chosen by minimum SSE
Map the channel to 1, 2 and 3 and run a single K-means with random initialisation
Standardise the numeric features, encode or handle the categorical one with a suitable method (e.g. K-prototypes), run multiple K-means++ restarts, and choose K by silhouette plus business review
Use KNN with k = 5 to find the segments
explanation: Unscaled spend would dominate the Euclidean distance, arbitrary integer codes give the categories a false order and distance, and a single random start risks a poor local optimum. Silhouette and business review guard against choosing K by SSE, which always favours more clusters. KNN is supervised and needs labels.
concept: Clustering design: scale, handle categoricals, restart, validate K.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Which task is an example of unsupervised learning?
options: Grouping customers by purchasing behaviour with no predefined labels
Predicting house prices from past sales
Classifying emails as spam or not using labelled examples
Predicting patient diabetes risk scores from labelled records
explanation: Unsupervised learning finds structure in data without target labels, as clustering does. The other tasks all learn a mapping to a known target from labelled examples, which is supervised learning.
concept: Supervised = labelled targets; unsupervised = structure without labels.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: For an OLS fit with residual vector e = y − Xθ*, which identity always holds?
options: e = 0 for every sample
XXᵀe = y
Xᵀe = 0, so the residuals are orthogonal to every column of X
explanation: Substituting the normal equations gives Xᵀe = Xᵀy − XᵀXθ* = 0, so ŷ is the orthogonal projection of y onto the column space of X. With an intercept column this also means the residuals sum to zero; zero residuals for every sample happen only with an exact fit.
concept: OLS residuals are orthogonal to the column space of X.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: If P(y = 1) = 0.2, what are the odds of y = 1?
explanation: Odds = p/(1 − p) = 0.2/0.8 = 0.25. The value 0.20 is the probability itself, and 4.00 is the odds of the opposite event.
concept: Odds = p/(1 − p).

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Gradient descent applied to linear regression with squared-error loss, updating on one sample at a time, is known as:
options: The perceptron convergence rule
The LMS (Widrow–Hoff) rule
The normal equations
Newton's method
explanation: The update θ ← θ − α(ŷ − y)x is the least-mean-squares (Widrow–Hoff) rule. The normal equations are the closed-form alternative, and Newton's method uses second derivatives.
concept: LMS = per-sample GD on squared error.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: In binary KNN classification, why is an odd k often preferred?
options: It prevents tied majority votes between the two classes
It guarantees higher accuracy than any even k
It makes the distance computation faster
It is required for the Euclidean distance to be valid
explanation: With two classes and an odd number of voters, one class always has a strict majority. An odd k does not guarantee better accuracy; k should still be chosen by validation.
concept: Odd k avoids voting ties in binary KNN.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Bayes' theorem for classification states that P(y | x) equals:
options: P(y | x)P(x)/P(y)
P(x)P(y)
P(x | y)/P(y)
P(x | y)P(y)/P(x)
explanation: The posterior is the likelihood times the prior, divided by the evidence P(x). For classification, P(x) is the same for every class, so the class can be chosen by comparing P(x | y)P(y) alone.
concept: Posterior = likelihood × prior / evidence.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: When is a hard-margin SVM appropriate rather than a soft-margin SVM?
options: Whenever the classes overlap
Whenever probability outputs are needed
Whenever there are more than two classes
Only when the training data are linearly separable (in the chosen feature space)
explanation: The hard-margin constraints y(wᵀx + b) ≥ 1 for all points have no solution when the classes overlap. Slack variables in the soft margin allow violations at a cost set by C. Neither form outputs probabilities.
concept: Hard margin requires separability; soft margin tolerates violations.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: For a function k to be a valid (Mercer) kernel, every Gram matrix Kᵢⱼ = k(xᵢ, xⱼ) must be:
options: Symmetric and positive semi-definite
Diagonal
Invertible with all entries positive
Upper triangular
explanation: A valid kernel is an inner product in some feature space, so every Gram matrix must be symmetric with no negative eigenvalues. For example, [[1, 2], [2, 1]] has eigenvalue −1 and cannot come from a valid kernel, even though all its entries are positive.
concept: Mercer: Gram matrices must be symmetric PSD.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: On which data is K-means most likely to give a poor clustering?
options: Three well-separated round blobs of similar size
Two compact groups far apart
Two interleaving crescent-shaped (moon) clusters
Four spherical clusters on standardised features
explanation: K-means carves space into convex regions around centroids, so it suits compact, roughly spherical clusters of similar size. Crescents are non-convex and interleaved, so the nearest-centroid split cuts across them.
concept: K-means assumes spherical, convex clusters.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: The silhouette score of a point lies in which range?
explanation: s = (b − a)/max(a, b) is close to 1 when the point is far closer to its own cluster, close to 0 on a border, and negative when it is closer to another cluster. Negative values are possible, so [0, 1] is wrong.
concept: Silhouette ∈ [−1, 1]; higher means better clustered.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: Why is F1 the harmonic, not the arithmetic, mean of precision and recall?
options: So that it equals accuracy on balanced data
So that it is always larger than both precision and recall
So that it ignores false negatives
So that the score stays low unless both precision and recall are reasonably high
explanation: The harmonic mean is pulled towards the smaller value: P = 1.0 and R = 0.1 give F1 ≈ 0.18, while the arithmetic mean is 0.55. That stops a model from scoring well by excelling at only one of the two. F1 can never exceed the larger of P and R.
concept: F1 punishes imbalance between precision and recall.

subject: Machine Learning
stem: What is the correct role of the test set when developing a model?
options: To tune hyperparameters, because it is the most realistic data
To give one final, unbiased estimate after all model and hyperparameter choices are fixed on training/validation data
To train the final model together with the validation data
To be checked after every epoch to decide when to stop
